name: Ohio

events.title: Statehood
events.text: Ohio became the 17th state on March 1, 1803. Congress gave it 1 seat in the House until the next apportionment.

events.title: 1810 census apportionment
events.text: After the 1810 census, Ohio's House delegation grew from 1 to 6 seats.

events.title: 1820 census apportionment
events.text: After the 1820 census, Ohio's House delegation grew from 6 to 14 seats.

events.title: 1830 census apportionment
events.text: After the 1830 census, Ohio's House delegation grew from 14 to 19 seats.

events.title: 1840 census apportionment
events.text: After the 1840 census, Ohio's House delegation grew from 19 to 21 seats.

events.title: 1850 census apportionment
events.text: After the 1850 census, Ohio kept 21 seats in the House.

events.title: 1860 census apportionment
events.text: After the 1860 census, Ohio's House delegation shrank from 21 to 19 seats.

events.title: 1870 census apportionment
events.text: After the 1870 census, Ohio's House delegation grew from 19 to 20 seats.

events.title: 1880 census apportionment
events.text: After the 1880 census, Ohio's House delegation grew from 20 to 21 seats.

events.title: 1890 census apportionment
events.text: After the 1890 census, Ohio kept 21 seats in the House.

events.title: 1900 census apportionment
events.text: After the 1900 census, Ohio kept 21 seats in the House.

events.title: 1910 census apportionment
events.text: After the 1910 census, Ohio's House delegation grew from 21 to 22 seats.

events.title: Some members elected at-large
events.text: In the 63rd Congress (1913–1915), Ohio elected one of its representatives statewide (at-large) and the rest by district.

events.title: 1930 census apportionment
events.text: After the 1930 census, Ohio's House delegation grew from 22 to 24 seats.

events.title: Some members elected at-large
events.text: In the 73rd through 77th Congresses (1933–1943), Ohio elected 2 of its representatives statewide (at-large) and the rest by district.

events.title: 1940 census apportionment
events.text: After the 1940 census, Ohio's House delegation shrank from 24 to 23 seats.

events.title: Some members elected at-large
events.text: In the 78th through 82nd Congresses (1943–1953), Ohio elected one of its representatives statewide (at-large) and the rest by district.

events.title: 1950 census apportionment
events.text: After the 1950 census, Ohio kept 23 seats in the House.

events.title: 1960 census apportionment
events.text: After the 1960 census, Ohio's House delegation grew from 23 to 24 seats.

events.title: Some members elected at-large
events.text: In the 88th through 89th Congresses (1963–1967), Ohio elected one of its representatives statewide (at-large) and the rest by district.

events.title: 1970 census apportionment
events.text: After the 1970 census, Ohio's House delegation shrank from 24 to 23 seats. Because districts must have nearly equal populations, the map was redrawn with the new census counts.

events.title: 1980 census apportionment
events.text: After the 1980 census, Ohio's House delegation shrank from 23 to 21 seats. Because districts must have nearly equal populations, the map was redrawn with the new census counts.

events.title: 1990 census apportionment
events.text: After the 1990 census, Ohio's House delegation shrank from 21 to 19 seats. Because districts must have nearly equal populations, the map was redrawn with the new census counts.

events.title: 2000 census apportionment
events.text: After the 2000 census, Ohio's House delegation shrank from 19 to 18 seats. Because districts must have nearly equal populations, the map was redrawn with the new census counts.

events.title: 2010 census apportionment
events.text: After the 2010 census, Ohio's House delegation shrank from 18 to 16 seats. Because districts must have nearly equal populations, the map was redrawn with the new census counts.

events.title: New congressional redistricting rules
events.text: Ohio voters approved Issue 1, a constitutional amendment requiring bipartisan support for a ten-year congressional map. A map passed without that support lasts only four years.

events.title: Map ruled unconstitutional but used
events.text: The Ohio Supreme Court ruled in January 2022 and again in July 2022 that the new congressional maps violated the state constitution. Because of election deadlines, the second map was used in the 2022 and 2024 elections.

events.title: 2020 census apportionment
events.text: After the 2020 census, Ohio's House delegation shrank from 16 to 15 seats. Because districts must have nearly equal populations, the map was redrawn with the new census counts.

events.title: New map required by the state constitution
events.text: Because the 2022 map passed without bipartisan support, Ohio's constitution limited it to four years. The Ohio Redistricting Commission approved a new map 7 to 0 on October 31, 2025, used from the 2026 election. Its largest changes were to the Cincinnati-based 1st and Toledo-based 9th Districts, and it keeps Summit County whole in the 13th District.

compactnessNote: Polsby-Popper compactness (4π × area ÷ perimeter²) measured on the projected district shapes. It describes shape only: coastlines, rivers and county lines lower it too, so a low score is not evidence of intent. "Irregular" marks the least compact 5% of district shapes in each census era nationally.

c013.text: New map drawn after the 1810 census, which raised Ohio's seats from 1 to 6. It was first used in the 1812 election.

c018.text: New map drawn after the 1820 census, which raised Ohio's seats from 6 to 14. It was first used in the 1822 election.

c022.text: Ohio's district lines were redrawn between censuses, first used in the 1830 election. The reason has not been researched yet.

c023.text: New map drawn after the 1830 census, which raised Ohio's seats from 14 to 19. It was first used in the 1832 election.

c028.text: New map drawn after the 1840 census, which raised Ohio's seats from 19 to 21. It was first used in the 1842 election.

c030.text: In March 1845 the General Assembly passed a new congressional map, the first time Ohio redrew its districts between censuses.

c033.text: New map drawn after the 1850 census, which left Ohio with 21 seats. It was first used in the 1852 election.

c038.text: New map drawn after the 1860 census, which cut Ohio's seats from 21 to 19. It was first used in the 1862 election.

c043.text: New map drawn after the 1870 census, which raised Ohio's seats from 19 to 20. It was first used in the 1872 election.

c046.text: The General Assembly passed a new congressional map in 1878, the first of several redraws through the early 1890s that gave Ohio a new map for most elections.

c047.text: The General Assembly elected in 1879 replaced the 1878 map with a new one for the 1880 election.

c048.text: New map drawn after the 1880 census, which raised Ohio's seats from 20 to 21. It was first used in the 1882 election.

c049.text: The General Assembly elected in 1883 replaced the 1882 post-census map with a new one for the 1884 election.

c050.text: The General Assembly elected in 1885 revised the 1884 map, and the new lines were used in the 1886 election.

c052.text: The General Assembly elected in 1889 redrew the congressional map in 1890, in time for that year's election.

c053.text: New map drawn after the 1890 census, which left Ohio with 21 seats. It was first used in the 1892 election.

c058.text: New map drawn after the 1900 census, which left Ohio with 21 seats. It was first used in the 1902 election.

c063.text: After the 1910 census raised Ohio's seats from 21 to 22, the state kept its existing districts and elected one member statewide (at-large).

c064.text: In 1912 Ohio elected its new 22nd seat statewide (at-large). For the 1914 election that seat was replaced by a new set of 22 districts.

c073.text: After the 1930 census raised Ohio's seats from 22 to 24, the state kept its existing districts and elected 2 members statewide (at-large).

c083.text: New map drawn after the 1950 census, which left Ohio with 23 seats. It was first used in the 1952 election.

c088.text: After the 1960 census raised Ohio's seats from 23 to 24, the state kept its existing districts and elected one member statewide (at-large).

c090.text: For the 1966 election Ohio replaced its statewide (at-large) seat with a new 24th District, so all 24 members were elected from districts.

c091.text: In Lucas v. Rhodes (1967) the Supreme Court reversed a ruling that had upheld Ohio's 1964 congressional map despite unequal populations. Ohio passed a new map in 1968, which a federal court approved.

c093.text: New map drawn after the 1970 census, which cut Ohio's seats from 24 to 23. It was first used in the 1972 election.

c098.text: New map drawn after the 1980 census, which cut Ohio's seats from 23 to 21. It was first used in the 1982 election.

c100.text: Ohio's district lines were redrawn between censuses, first used in the 1986 election. The reason has not been researched yet.

c103.text: New map drawn after the 1990 census, which cut Ohio's seats from 21 to 19. It was first used in the 1992 election.

c108.text: New map drawn after the 2000 census, which cut Ohio's seats from 19 to 18. It was first used in the 2002 election.

c113.text: New map drawn after the 2010 census, which cut Ohio's seats from 18 to 16. It was first used in the 2012 election.

c115.text: Not a new map: the historical boundary records show only slight differences in 3 districts from the previous Congress, and no statewide redistricting is recorded for this election.

c118.text: New map drawn after the 2020 census, which cut Ohio's seats from 16 to 15. It was first used in the 2022 election.

c120.text: New map following: New map required by the state constitution. Because the 2022 map passed without bipartisan support, Ohio's constitution limited it to four years. The Ohio Redistricting Commission approved a new map 7 to 0 on October 31, 2025, used from the 2026 election. Its largest changes were to the Cincinnati-based 1st and Toledo-based 9th Districts, and it keeps Summit County whole in the 13th District.
